# Introduction to Data Visualisation with `matplotlib`

On this page we will look at two things:

- data visualisation

- procedural programming vs object oriented programming *from the point of view of using a Python package that you did not write*. E.g. you will see the "user side" of a library that allows both a procedural and object oriented approach.

Data visualisation means showing data *visually*. Our brains are very good at seeing the relationship between variables when we look at the data as *graphs* instead of looking at numbers in a table.

We explore data visualisation with the `matplotlib` library. I want to show you a real world use case of Procedural Programming AND Object Oriented Programming. `matplotlib` has a Procedural Programming interface, where we make our plots step-by-step with functions. It also as Object Oriented interface, where we create instances of graph classes and then use these to make our visualisations.

First, we will import some data. We will use the `pandas` libary to do this. We will use this library more in the next class, for now, just think of it like a really really really advanced Microsoft Excel.

Here is how we read in a dataset as a *Pandas DataFrame*. This dataset shows how many airline passengers there were worldwide between 1949 and 1960.

```{python}
# Import `pandas`.
import pandas as pd

# This reads in the file and stores it as a variable.
df = pd.read_csv('data/airline_passengers.csv')

df
```

The simplest way to get data out of data out of a dataframe is to use the name of the columns:

```{python}
df['Thousands of Passengers']
```

```{python}
df['Month']
```

We can also do Boolean indexing, just like on a NumPy array:

```{python}
# Make a Boolean array.
bigger_than_400_boolean_arr = df['Thousands of Passengers'] > 400

# Use Boolean indexing.
df[bigger_than_400_boolean_arr]
```

As a quick aside, Pandas dataframes are objects, written in their source code in the Object Oriented Programming style. 

They have attributes and methods. For instance we can get just the `name` of each column using:

```{python}
df['Thousands of Passengers'].name
```

## Procedural Plotting with `matplotlib`

We have already seen `plt.hist()` - this is great when we want to look at how *one* variable is distributed:

```{python}
# Import `matplotlib`, rename it as `plt`.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.hist(df['Thousands of Passengers'])
```

A few things are pretty ugly about this - we see lots of junk above the plot, and our plot has not title or labels on the axes.

Let's fix this:

```{python}
plt.hist(df['Thousands of Passengers'])

# Add some axis labels.
plt.xlabel('Thousands of Passengers')
plt.ylabel('Count')

# Add a title.
plt.title('Thousands of Passengers')

# This stops the junk at the top of the plot.
plt.show()
```

Nice!

You'll notice here that we are using *functions*. You can read the code in the cell like this:

`plt.hist()` → Draw a histogram.

`plt.xlabel()` → Set the X-axis label.

`plt.ylabel()` → Set the Y-axis label.

`plt.title()` → Set the plot title.

`plt.show()` → Display the plot.

Using `matplotlib` this way is in the *procedural programming style*.


## Object Oriented Plotting with `matplotlib`

Let's have a look at the same plot, but made using `matplotlib`'s Object Oriented Style:

```{python}
# Create a figure and axes. These are instances of classes.
# This line of conde makes the instances.
fig, ax = plt.subplots()

# Plot the histogram (notice that now we are using *methods* of the axes objects, instead of functions).
ax.hist(df['Thousands of Passengers'])

# Add axis labels (notice that now we are using *methods* of the axes objects, instead of functions).
ax.set_xlabel('Thousands of Passengers')
ax.set_ylabel('Count')

# Add a title (notice that now we are using *methods* of the axes objects, instead of functions).
ax.set_title('Thousands of Passengers')

# Display the plot.
plt.show()
```

As the comments in the cell above say - this approach uses *objects* and *methods* instead of functions. Here is how to read the code in the cell above:

`fig` → An instance of the `Figure` class (the entire canvas).

`ax` → An instance of the `Axes` class (the plotting area).

`ax.hist()` → Ask the `Axes` object to draw a histogram.

`ax.set_xlabel()` → Set the X-axis label of that `Axes` object.

`ax.set_title()` → Set the title of that `Axes` object.

Notice that we still use `plt.show()` (e.g. the function) in the last line of the cell above, even though the rest of the code is Object Oriented. In `matplotlib`, but also in Python in general, we can mix and match the Procedural and Object Oriented Coding styles - do whatever works best for a specific context!


## Other Types of Graph

Looking at one variable is useful - we need to do it before we do any statistical analysis! But we also get useful information from plotting many variables together. This makes it possible to see **trends**, **patterns** and **relationships** between the variables.

A simple way to look at how two variables are related is to use a *scatter plot*.

We can do this in the procedural style, with the following code:

```{python}
# Make the scatterplot.
plt.scatter(x = df['Month'],
            y = df['Thousands of Passengers'])

# Add axis labels.
plt.xlabel('Month')
plt.ylabel('Thousands of Passengers')

# Show the plot.
plt.show()
```

The x-axis looks weird - there are too many labels to show on the plot. 

To fix this, we can slice the dataframe column, just we can with a NumPy array (actually Pandas dataframes are built *from* NumPy arrays!):

```{python}
df['Month'][::20]
```

We can use this slice of the data, with the `plt.xticks()` function, to make the x-axis show less labels:

```{python}
# Make the scatterplot.
plt.scatter(x = df['Month'],
            y = df['Thousands of Passengers'])

# Add axis labels.
plt.xlabel('Month')
plt.ylabel('Thousands of Passengers')

# Tidy up the x-axis.
plt.xticks(df['Month'][::20])

# Show the plot.
plt.show()
```

This makes it much easier to read the graph, and nicer to look at!

What do you think the graph shows?

It is possible to see a clear trend on this plot - I guess here would could use the phrase ["number go up"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_Go_Up).

But right now each point on the graph shows the data for one month. The trend *between* the years is easy to see, but the relationship between months that are close to each other is a bit messy.

A better way to show this data is to use the `plt.plot()` function. This will try to plot the data we give it as a continuous line:

```{python}
# Make the line plot.
plt.plot(df['Month'],
         df['Thousands of Passengers'])

# Add axis labels.
plt.xlabel('Month')
plt.ylabel('Thousands of Passengers')

# Tidy up the x-axis.
plt.xticks(df['Month'][::20])

# Show the plot.
plt.show()
```

<!-- #region -->
Now we can see that overall the number of passengers goes up, but also the *fluctuations* get bigger in later years.

**Take a moment to think**: what do you think those fluctuations are? What is the real life explanation here?


### Making the same scatterplot and lineplot, using OOP

Just for completeness, here is how you make these two plots using the `matplotlib` OOP style:
<!-- #endregion -->

```{python}
# Create a Figure and Axes.
fig, ax = plt.subplots()

# Make the scatterplot.
ax.scatter(x = df['Month'],
           y = df['Thousands of Passengers'])

# Add axis labels.
ax.set_xlabel('Month')
ax.set_ylabel('Thousands of Passengers')

# Tidy up the x-axis.
ax.set_xticks(df['Month'][::20])

# Show the plot.
plt.show()
```

```{python}
# Create a Figure and Axes.
fig, ax = plt.subplots()

# Make the line plot.
ax.plot(df['Month'],
        df['Thousands of Passengers'])

# Add axis labels.
ax.set_xlabel('Month')
ax.set_ylabel('Thousands of Passengers')

# Tidy up the x-axis.
ax.set_xticks(df['Month'][::20])

# Show the plot.
plt.show()
```
